title: Who decides?
hook: a pope, councils of bishops, synods, or congregations: churches order authority differently

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four marks: one, holy, catholic, apostolic, said together and explained differently.

The argument has traveled all the way from Antioch to Jerusalem. The church is young; the question is big: must believers who aren't Jewish take on the whole law of Moses, circumcision included, to follow Jesus? Good people stand on both sides. So, in the fifteenth chapter of Acts, the apostles and elders come together. There's much disputing. Peter tells what he's seen. Paul and Barnabas tell their stories. Then James gives his judgment. And the letter they send out carries a sentence worth hearing slowly. Behind it sits today's question: who decides?

The letter says: "For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us." Both: the Spirit, and a room of people who argued. Churches across the traditions hold that hope: that their decisions can be human and holy at once. But they've built that room very differently. Catholics look to the pope, the bishop of Rome, as Peter's successor, with the bishops in communion with him; they read Jesus's words, "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church," as founding that office. The Orthodox are governed by bishops in councils and synods, with patriarchs who lead without a single head over all, and see the council in Acts as their pattern. Presbyterian and Reformed churches are led by elders, ruling together in local sessions and wider assemblies; they point to the elders in that chapter. Baptists and other congregational churches gather the members to decide, trusting the Spirit to speak through the whole body, and notice that the apostles and elders acted with "the whole church." Each can read Acts fifteen and see its own room. Under it all sits something Jesus said when two disciples asked for the best seats and the others were angry. Rulers lord it over people. "But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister." A minister, in that old English, is a servant. Paul adds: "Let all things be done decently and in order." In Christian teaching, order is meant to serve love: so the hungry get fed, the gospel gets told, and nobody gets trampled.
screen: `IT SEEMED GOOD TO THE SPIRIT AND TO US.` · `POPE AND BISHOPS; COUNCILS AND SYNODS.` · `ELDERS; THE WHOLE CONGREGATION.` · `THE GREAT ONE IS THE SERVANT.` · then, large: `DECENTLY AND IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind whoever carries the decisions where you belong, a pastor or priest, a bishop, elders, a council, or, outside a church, a manager, a teacher, a parent. Picture them in a hard meeting where good people disagree. If you pray, ask that their decisions seem good to the Holy Spirit and to them, and that they lead by serving; if you don't, just hold them kindly in that hard room.
Who decides? Popes and bishops, councils and synods, elders, whole congregations: different shapes of one hope, that the Spirit and the people agree.
Your line: order for love. The great one among you is the servant. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics are led by the pope and bishops, Orthodox churches by bishops in synods, Presbyterian and Reformed churches by elders in sessions and assemblies, and Baptist and other congregational churches by the gathered members; churches often pray for their leaders by name in worship.

original.note: Greek: overseer — the New Testament word that English renders as bishop.

what it means: churches order authority differently, through a pope and bishops, synods, elders or congregations, each hoping the Spirit and the people agree.
what a scholar hears: episkopos, overseer, is the word the King James renders bishop. Acts 15 is read by each tradition as its own pattern.

chat.says: In Acts 15, how did the church settle the big argument about the law of Moses?
options: The apostles and elders met, argued, and wrote: it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us.
Paul overruled the Jerusalem church on his own and sent the letter out alone.
It didn't; Acts says the meeting broke up and each church went its own way.
chat.meaning: In Acts 15 the apostles and elders gather, dispute, and hear Peter, Paul, Barnabas and James. Their letter says it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us.

Antioch.meaning: the city whose church carried the question to Jerusalem

Barnabas.meaning: Paul's companion, who told his story at the meeting

synods.meaning: church gatherings, often of bishops, that decide matters

patriarchs.meaning: senior Orthodox bishops who lead their churches

notes: Acts 15 framing: the question (whether Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, 15:1, 15:5) is described neutrally; Jewish law is not used as a foil. Confirm tone.
'Good people stand on both sides' is interpretive; Acts 15:5 names believers of the sect of the Pharisees; the script does not name them, to avoid a foil. Confirm.

Polity summaries (Catholic papacy and Matthew 16:18; Orthodox conciliarity without a single head of jurisdiction; Presbyterian sessions and assemblies; congregational polity and Acts 15:22) are characterizations; confirm fairness. Methodist, Anglican, Lutheran polities not named for length.
'A minister, in that old English, is a servant' — gloss of KJV 'minister' (Greek diakonos); confirm.
Trapdoor: ἐπίσκοπος/πρεσβύτερος as the words behind 'bishop' and 'priest' is a standard derivation; confirm.
Mark 10:35–45 context: James and John ask for seats at his right and left; the ten are indignant. Confirm the summary.
